paragraphs: When data contain many features, selecting useful features individually can produce unstable results. Grouping features can reduce estimation variability, improve selection stability, and make a model easier to interpret. OSCAR combines sparse modeling with automatic grouping, using two regularization terms to encourage these behaviors. Its practical drawback is the computational expense of fitting the model.

The paper develops a faster OSCAR solver using accelerated gradient methods. Its central contribution is a simple iterative procedure that merges groups to solve the projection step required by the optimizer. This makes a previously expensive operation more efficient and addresses the computational obstacle to using automatic feature grouping with many input dimensions.

The authors report that empirical time complexity drops from roughly cubic through fifth-power dependence on the number of features to linear dependence. This is a reported empirical scaling result. Experiments on synthetic and real data also show that OSCAR is competitive as a sparse modeling method while retaining its additional ability to discover feature groups.
icml-2011-efficient-sparse-modeling-with.tldr: An accelerated solver makes OSCAR’s combination of sparse modeling and automatic feature grouping substantially more efficient in reported experiments.

paragraphs: GoDec separates a matrix into three parts: a low-rank component, a sparse component, and remaining noise. The low-rank part captures structure that can be represented compactly, while the sparse part accounts for a relatively small collection of entries. The goal is to estimate these two structured components efficiently even when the observed matrix also contains noise.

The algorithm alternates between two updates. It subtracts the current sparse estimate and finds a low-rank approximation, then subtracts the current low-rank estimate and finds a sparse approximation. Bilateral random projections can substantially accelerate this process. The paper also develops a matrix-completion variant, extending the approach to recovering a matrix from incomplete observations.

The analysis establishes convergence of the objective to a local minimum and linear convergence of the component estimates to local optima. It also examines how the components and noise affect convergence speed and robustness. Empirical comparisons with matrix decomposition and completion methods support GoDec’s efficiency, robustness, and effectiveness; the convergence claims remain local.
icml-2011-godec-randomized-lowrank-spars.tldr: GoDec alternates low-rank and sparse approximations to decompose noisy matrices efficiently, with local convergence guarantees and supportive empirical results.

paragraphs: Infinite SVM addresses classification among multiple categories when complex data may require different local decision rules. It combines a collection of large-margin kernel machines within a Dirichlet process mixture. This brings together two capabilities: handling an unknown number of mixture components and representing nonlinear patterns within the portions of data associated with those components.

The Bayesian nonparametric part handles uncertainty about how many components the mixture needs. The kernel machines provide the ability to capture local nonlinear relationships robustly. The model therefore connects flexibility in the mixture’s structure with flexibility in its classification rules, rather than treating the number of components and the form of each classifier as unrelated design choices.

The authors develop an efficient variational algorithm for posterior inference, making the combined model learnable in practice. Experiments on synthetic data and real Flickr image classification datasets demonstrate advantages over a Dirichlet process mixture of generalized linear models and other benchmarks. These findings support the proposed combination in the evaluated classification settings.
icml-2011-infinite-svm-a-dirichlet-proce.tldr: Infinite SVM combines an adaptable mixture structure with large-margin kernel classifiers to model complex multiclass data.

paragraphs: Online learning updates a model as training examples arrive. Many approaches judge success through classification accuracy, but that measure can be inappropriate when classes occur at very different frequencies. This paper instead targets the area under the ROC curve, or AUC, a measure widely used to evaluate classification with imbalanced data.

Optimizing AUC creates a different learning problem because the loss compares pairs of examples from different classes. An update therefore depends on relationships between examples, rather than only on the newly arriving example. The authors use reservoir sampling to address this obstacle and construct two online algorithms that can work with the pairwise objective.

Both algorithms come with theoretical performance guarantees, and extensive experiments support their effectiveness and efficiency at maximizing AUC. The contribution is a way to align an online learner’s optimization target with an evaluation measure suited to class imbalance. It also shows how sampling can help bridge the gap between learning from individual arrivals and optimizing comparisons across examples.
icml-2011-online-auc-maximization-33c2fa.tldr: Two online algorithms use reservoir sampling to optimize pairwise AUC losses, with theoretical guarantees and supportive experiments.

paragraphs: The paper develops a factor-analysis model whose structure is organized as a tree. Its aim is to learn relationships within high-dimensional data while also inferring the tree’s size and shape. Both the number of levels and the branching structure are therefore part of what the model learns.

The central ingredient is a tree-structured multiplicative gamma process, introduced to infer tree depth. The authors combine it with a nested Chinese restaurant process so that the model can infer both depth and width nonparametrically. These two components address complementary aspects of the hierarchy: how far it extends and how it branches. Together, they support learning the overall tree structure from data.

The work also examines theoretical properties of the new process and introduces an MCMC sampler for inference. The inferred tree is used to discover relationships among high-dimensional observations. Applications to compressive sensing and interpolation of incomplete images illustrate how the same structured model can support reconstruction tasks as well as the organization of data.
icml-2011-tree-structured-infinite-spars.tldr: A Bayesian tree-based factor model learns both hierarchy depth and branching structure to represent high-dimensional data and support reconstruction tasks.

paragraphs: The paper studies finite stochastic partial monitoring, where a learner must make decisions using incomplete feedback. It introduces an anytime algorithm with near-optimal regret across problem instances. Regret measures the cumulative cost of learning compared with a reference decision strategy, so controlling its growth captures how quickly the learner makes effective use of feedback.

The algorithm achieves minimax regret up to logarithmic factors for both easy and hard problem classes. For easy problems, it also obtains logarithmic instance-specific regret. Its distinctive feature is adaptation within a problem: when the opponent’s strategy lies in an easy region of the strategy space, regret grows at the rate associated with an easy problem.

This distinction matters because a problem’s worst-case classification need not describe the difficulty of the strategy actually encountered. As an application, the authors establish square-root-in-time regret for dynamic pricing under additional assumptions, even though that problem is classified as hard. The pricing guarantee is conditional on those assumptions, while illustrating the benefit of adapting to favorable regions.
icml-2012-an-adaptive-algorithm-for-fini.tldr: An adaptive partial-monitoring algorithm achieves near-optimal regret and can exploit easy regions even within generally hard problems.

paragraphs: Active learning chooses which examples should be labeled to reduce labeling effort. Sequential methods choose one example at a time, using each new answer to guide the next choice. When labels can be obtained in parallel, selecting an entire batch is more convenient, but it removes the opportunity to respond to answers within that batch.

This paper builds a batch method around existing sequential policies. It uses Monte Carlo simulation to estimate which examples a sequential policy would select across several steps. It then seeks a batch whose collection of examples matches that estimated selection distribution. The objective is to approximate the behavior of an effective sequential policy when several labeling requests must be issued together.

The resulting selection problem, called bounded coordinated matching, is NP-hard in general. The authors provide an efficient greedy solution with approximation bounds inherited from supermodular minimization theory. Experiments on eight benchmark datasets show that the approach is highly effective, supporting simulation and coordinated selection as a practical route from sequential policies to batch learning.
icml-2012-batch-active-learning-via-coor.tldr: A batch active-learning method simulates sequential selection and uses coordinated matching to choose effective groups of labeling requests.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether Bayesian posterior samples can be generated while accessing only a small mini-batch of data for each sample. Stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics already addresses this computational constraint, but its slow mixing can make it difficult to move efficiently through the posterior distribution. The authors extend that approach to improve this trade-off.

Their construction uses the Bayesian Central Limit Theorem to connect sampling behavior with a normal approximation to the posterior. At high mixing rates, the algorithm samples from that approximation. At slower mixing rates, it behaves like stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics equipped with a preconditioning matrix. The two regimes therefore offer different relationships between exploration speed and the posterior distribution being approximated.

The method also resembles Fisher scoring with stochastic gradients, giving it an additional role as an efficient optimizer during burn-in. This matters because the initial movement toward a useful region and subsequent sampling are both part of posterior computation. The fast regime specifically targets a normal approximation, which is central to interpreting its sampling behavior.
icml-2012-bayesian-posterior-sampling-vi.tldr: Stochastic gradient Fisher scoring combines mini-batch posterior sampling with fast Gaussian approximation and efficient optimization during burn-in.

paragraphs: Web sources often publish information that is copied or rephrased elsewhere. As related material spreads, it can become a trend across a collection of sites. This paper addresses the problem of finding sources that publish information relevant to such a trend before other sources do, making timing central to the identification of trend setters.

The proposed method has two connected purposes: finding trends that dominate a pool of web sources and identifying early publishers of information associated with those trends. Linking these tasks gives the early-publication question a specific context. A source is examined in relation to a shared trend, allowing publication order to help distinguish its role within that trend.

The authors describe the method as simple and efficient and validate it using real data from influential technology news feeds. This provides evidence for applying the approach to actual web publishing activity. The contribution is a way to organize repeated information into trends and then identify which sources were early in publishing the material relevant to them.
icml-2012-canonical-trends-detecting-tre.tldr: A simple method identifies dominant web trends and the sources that publish related information earliest.

paragraphs: The paper studies a bandit setting in which earning a reward and collecting information can involve different choices. On each round, one arm supplies the reward added to the decision maker’s total, while another arm can be explored to reveal its value. The reward from the exploited arm need not itself be observed.

The authors develop algorithms for this separation and show that dependence on the number of arms can improve substantially over the standard square-root dependence. The improvement depends on how the arms’ reward sequences behave. They establish a significant gain over existing algorithms for piecewise stationary stochastic bandits, where reward behavior is stable within segments but can change between them.

The algorithms use non-uniform sampling, assigning different exploration frequencies to different arms. The paper shows that this is essential for success in the adversarial setting considered. Simulations inspired by ultra-wideband channel selection indicate practical applicability. Together, the results show how separating information gathering from reward collection can change the learning problem and the benefits available from targeted exploration.
icml-2012-decoupling-exploration-and-exp.tldr: Separating exploration from reward collection enables improved bandit guarantees under suitable reward behavior, using non-uniform exploration.

paragraphs: The paper develops optimization methods for a broad class of matrix problems using nuclear norm regularization. Its focus is making individual optimization steps inexpensive while keeping the evolving matrix representation compact. This is especially relevant to matrix completion, where the learned matrix must also support efficient predictions for entries that have not been observed.

The approach combines low-rank stochastic subgradients with incremental updates to a singular value decomposition. These operations are implemented through optimized dense linear algebra on small matrices and can be parallelized. The combination connects the structure of each update with the structure of the stored solution, allowing the algorithm to maintain a low-rank factorization throughout optimization.

That factorization serves two practical purposes: it can be held conveniently in memory, and its factors can be multiplied efficiently to produce matrix-completion predictions. Empirical comparisons show that the resulting algorithms are highly competitive with several contemporary solvers. The contribution therefore concerns the cost of optimization, storage, and prediction together, rather than treating computational efficiency as only the number of iterations.
icml-2012-efficient-and-practical-stocha.tldr: Low-rank stochastic updates and incremental SVD make nuclear-norm matrix optimization inexpensive per iteration and compact in memory.

paragraphs: In aptitude testing and crowdsourcing, several unknowns can be intertwined: which answers are correct, how difficult the questions are, and how capable the participants are. This paper introduces a probabilistic graphical model that represents all three together. The aim is to infer these quantities jointly from responses, including when the correct answers are initially unknown.

The authors also develop an adaptive scheme for deciding which question to ask next. It greedily minimizes expected model entropy, using the model’s uncertainty to guide the next request. Because the choice depends on earlier responses, the allocation of questions changes as information accumulates. This connects the estimation problem directly to how new evidence is collected.

Experiments confirm that the model can infer the required parameters and show that adaptive testing reaches the same accuracy with fewer questions than a static test. The reported result gives a concrete meaning to more efficient resource allocation: in those experiments, dynamically selecting questions reduced the amount of questioning needed to attain a given level of accuracy.
icml-2012-how-to-grade-a-test-without-kn.tldr: A joint model of answers, question difficulty, and participant ability supports adaptive testing that uses fewer questions at the same experimental accuracy.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization searches for good inputs to an unknown function that is expensive to evaluate. Sequential selection can use every completed evaluation to inform the next choice. Batch selection allows evaluations to run concurrently, reducing experimental time, but choices within a batch are made without all the feedback that sequential selection would have received.

The paper combines these modes using a Gaussian process as the posterior estimator. Its hybrid algorithm examines the current state and switches dynamically between sequential evaluation and batches of variable size. The central idea is to let the available information determine how much evaluation work to launch together, balancing informative choices with the opportunity for parallel execution.

The authors provide theoretical justification and evaluate the method on eight benchmark optimization problems. They report speedups of up to 78 percent relative to a purely sequential policy, without significant optimization-performance loss in those experiments. The result supports adaptive batching as a way to capture substantial time savings while preserving much of the benefit of feedback-informed selection.
icml-2012-hybrid-batch-bayesian-optimiza.tldr: A hybrid Bayesian optimizer dynamically chooses sequential or batch evaluation, achieving reported speedups of up to 78 percent without significant performance loss.

paragraphs: Networks can contain information both in their connections and in the features attached to individual nodes. The Latent Multi-group Membership Graph model brings these two sources together. It allows each node to belong to multiple hidden groups, giving the model a way to represent overlapping memberships within the same network.

Each latent group models both the occurrence of links and the structure of node features. This ties the explanation of who connects to whom to the explanation of what those nodes are like. Multiple membership is important to that representation because a node can participate in several groups, each contributing to the model’s account of its connections and attributes.

The resulting model can summarize network structure, predict links, and predict missing node features. The authors derive efficient inference and learning algorithms and evaluate predictive performance on social and document networks. These tasks illustrate the value of a shared representation: the same learned group structure can support understanding the network and filling in different kinds of missing information.
icml-2012-latent-multi-group-membership-.tldr: A network model uses overlapping latent groups to jointly represent links and node features and predict missing information.

paragraphs: The paper revisits spectral learning for latent-variable models described through observable operators. Its central finding is that these operators can be recovered by minimizing a loss defined on a finite subspace of the domain. This gives spectral learning an optimization interpretation and makes the choice of a local loss part of the learning procedure.

From this perspective, the authors derive a non-convex optimization resembling the spectral method and propose a regularized convex relaxation. The relaxation introduces a continuous regularization parameter. This supplies a smoother way to adjust model complexity than choosing the discrete number of states used by the original method, creating another means of balancing fit and complexity.

In practice, the continuous control is shown to yield a better accuracy–complexity trade-off. The paper also proves that a randomized strategy for choosing the local loss succeeds with high probability in general. Together, these results connect an alternative formulation of spectral learning with both a practical model-selection advantage and a probabilistic guarantee for constructing the local objective.
icml-2012-local-loss-optimization-in-ope.tldr: An optimization view of spectral learning yields a regularized convex alternative with finer control over model complexity.

paragraphs: Binary classifiers are often trained by minimizing a convex surrogate loss, even though their eventual quality is judged by how often they assign the wrong label. This paper examines how well those two objectives align for linear predictors. Its focus is the classification error that can be guaranteed after minimizing a chosen surrogate.

The main result compares convex losses using the best achievable margin error as the reference quantity. Under this comparison, hinge loss provides essentially the strongest possible bound on the resulting linear predictor’s misclassification rate among convex surrogates. The qualification matters: the result concerns this particular guarantee for linear classification and does not assert that hinge loss wins every empirical comparison.

The authors also establish lower bounds for particular convex surrogate losses. These reveal qualitative differences between commonly used training objectives, showing that their classification guarantees need not be interchangeable. The paper’s contribution is a sharper theoretical account of how surrogate choice constrains the relationship between successful loss minimization and low classification error.
icml-2012-minimizing-the-misclassificati.tldr: For linear binary classifiers, hinge loss gives essentially the best convex-surrogate error bound in terms of achievable margin error.

paragraphs: Model-based Bayesian reinforcement learning provides a formal way to reason about acting in an unknown environment while accounting for uncertainty. It incorporates the value of learning about the environment into decision making. Explicitly solving this problem can produce a combinatorial explosion, which motivates simpler heuristic methods that remain computationally manageable.

The paper introduces BOLT, a simple and almost deterministic heuristic that is optimistic about the environment’s transition function. Transitions describe how actions move the agent between states, so optimism enters the model through its expectations about those movements. The method uses this local treatment of transitions as a way to guide decisions under uncertainty.

The authors analyze BOLT’s sample complexity and prove that, for certain parameter settings, it is near-optimal in the Bayesian sense with high probability. Both the parameter condition and the Bayesian comparison are part of the guarantee. Experiments highlight differences from earlier methods, complementing the analysis with evidence about how this particular form of optimism changes behavior.
icml-2012-near-optimal-brl-using-optimis.tldr: BOLT uses optimistic transition estimates to obtain a simple Bayesian reinforcement-learning heuristic with conditional near-optimality guarantees.

paragraphs: The paper establishes that herding can be understood as a standard conditional gradient algorithm for convex optimization. In this formulation, the algorithm minimizes a quadratic discrepancy between moments. The equivalence turns a procedure for constructing approximations into an optimization method with a recognizable objective and access to an existing body of convergence analysis.

This connection lets the authors apply convergence results from convex optimization and propose faster alternatives for approximating integrals in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. The practical question becomes how different optimization variants behave on the integration task. The paper investigates these alternatives through numerical simulations, using the shared formulation to compare their behavior.

The experiments indicate that integral approximation can be improved, while original herding more often approaches the maximum entropy distribution. These are distinct observed tendencies: improving the integration objective does not necessarily preserve the original procedure’s distributional preference. The result therefore clarifies both how herding can be accelerated for one task and what its original learning behavior appears to favor.
icml-2012-on-the-equivalence-between-her.tldr: Viewing herding as conditional gradient optimization yields convergence tools and faster integration variants while revealing differences in distributional bias.

paragraphs: The paper studies how many samples are needed to estimate the optimal action-value function in a discounted Markov decision process. The setting assumes access to a generative model. The target is an estimate within a specified error tolerance with a specified high probability, making sample requirements depend on both accuracy and confidence.

For model-based value iteration, the authors establish an upper bound proportional to N log(N/δ) divided by (1−γ)³ε². Here N is the number of state-action pairs, γ is the discount factor, ε is the error tolerance, and δ is the allowed failure probability. The expression describes how larger problems, tighter accuracy requirements, and longer effective reward horizons increase the required data.

A matching lower bound shows that every reinforcement-learning algorithm faces the same order of sample requirements for this estimation problem. Thus, the upper bound matches the fundamental limit in all four parameters. Both bounds improve the stated prior results in their dependence on the discount factor, with the conclusion applying to the generative-model setting analyzed.
icml-2012-on-the-sample-complexity-of-re.tldr: Matching sample-complexity bounds characterize the data needed to estimate optimal action values in discounted MDPs with a generative model.

paragraphs: The paper studies poisoning attacks that introduce deliberately constructed examples into an SVM’s training data to increase its later test error. The motivation is that learning methods commonly assume naturally generated or well-behaved training data. In security-sensitive settings, an adversary may instead shape part of that data to influence the learned classifier.

The authors show that an attacker can predict, to some extent, how malicious inputs change the SVM decision function. Their method uses gradient ascent, deriving the gradient from properties of the SVM’s optimal solution. The approach also supports kernels, allowing malicious points to be constructed in the original input space even when the classifier uses a nonlinear kernel.

Experiments show that the procedure reliably finds good local maxima of the non-convex validation-error surface and substantially worsens the trained classifier’s test error. The local nature of these maxima is part of the reported result. The work demonstrates how sensitivity of a fitted model to training data can become a practical attack mechanism when that data can be manipulated.
icml-2012-poisoning-attacks-against-supp.tldr: Gradient-based poisoning exploits how SVM solutions respond to training data, producing attacks that substantially increase test error in experiments.

paragraphs: The paper examines shortest-path distances in graphs built by connecting randomly sampled data points to their nearest neighbors. The samples come from a density on a Euclidean space, and the graphs may be weighted or unweighted. The question is what distance these graph paths represent as the number of sampled points grows without bound.

For unweighted nearest-neighbor graphs, the authors prove convergence to a distance function on the underlying space whose properties are detrimental to machine learning. This makes the limiting geometry the central concern. Increasing the sample size leads toward a well-defined distance, but the existence of that limit does not make its properties desirable for learning.

The paper also studies shortest-path behavior in weighted versions of these graphs. Considering both forms draws attention to graph construction as part of the meaning of a computed distance. The stated negative result for unweighted graphs warns that a shortest path through sampled neighbors can converge to an unsuitable notion of separation even as sampling becomes increasingly dense.
icml-2012-shortest-path-distance-in-rand.tldr: Shortest-path distances in unweighted random nearest-neighbor graphs converge to a limiting distance with undesirable properties for machine learning.

paragraphs: Learning a distance or similarity function can strongly affect classification. The paper contrasts its approach with methods that learn positive-semidefinite Mahalanobis distances for local nearest-neighbor classification, where a theoretical connection between the learned metric and classification performance is absent in the account given. Its goal is to build that connection into similarity learning.

Using a formal framework of good similarities, the authors learn a linear similarity without requiring positive semidefiniteness. The similarity is optimized in a nonlinear feature space and designed for a global linear classifier. This aligns the learned similarity with its intended classification use, while allowing a broader form than the constrained distance functions discussed.

The authors prove stability and use it to derive a generalization bound on classification error. Experiments across several datasets support effectiveness relative to contemporary methods and provide evidence of speed, resistance to overfitting, and very sparse models. The theoretical contribution links learning to classification accuracy, while the empirical results address whether that link comes with useful practical behavior.
icml-2012-similarity-learning-for-provab.tldr: A similarity-learning method targets sparse global linear classification and provides a stability-based generalization bound.

paragraphs: Canonical correlation analysis seeks relationships between two collections of measurements. In genomics, those collections can arise from different assays performed on the same patient samples. Many measured variables make sparsity useful, but both classical CCA and its sparse linear variants remain limited in the nonlinear relationships they can uncover.

The paper introduces two approaches to high-dimensional nonparametric CCA, drawing on developments in nonparametric regression. Their aim is to expand the kinds of cross-collection relationships that CCA can represent while addressing high dimensionality. The authors provide estimation procedures for both approaches and analyze their theoretical properties in that setting.

Extensive simulations and experiments with genomic data demonstrate effectiveness at discovering nonlinear correlations. This matters because reducing the number of selected variables does not by itself remove the restrictions of a linear model. The contribution addresses the form of the relationship as well as the dimensionality of the data, offering ways to find associations that linear CCA has limited ability to capture.
icml-2012-sparse-additive-functional-and.tldr: Two high-dimensional nonparametric CCA methods discover nonlinear relationships between paired measurement sets, with theory and genomic-data experiments.

paragraphs: Extreme events such as heatwaves, strong wind gusts, and sudden topic bursts can be the main quantities of interest in time-series analysis. The paper emphasizes that these data often have heavy-tailed distributions, creating a mismatch with normal-distribution assumptions. Extreme events also offer relatively little historical evidence because the events being modeled are uncommon.

Sparse-GEV is a latent-state model grounded in extreme-value modeling. It learns sparse temporal dependencies across multiple extreme-value time series and uses them for prediction. The sparse structure focuses the model on a limited set of temporal relationships, while the extreme-value foundation addresses the distributional character of the events that motivate the task.

The authors identify the approach as among the first models to learn such sparse dependencies across multivariate extreme-value series. Experiments on synthetic, climate, and Twitter data show superior performance to the evaluated Granger-causality, copula, and transfer-entropy approaches. These results support modeling temporal relationships and extreme-event distributions together in the tested settings.
icml-2012-sparse-gev-sparse-latent-space.tldr: Sparse-GEV combines extreme-value modeling with sparse temporal dependencies to predict related extreme-event time series.

paragraphs: Prediction can be difficult because the output contains many dimensions, even when the input is relatively small. This paper focuses on that situation and also allows high-dimensional inputs. Its approach is to select a small subset of output dimensions, called landmarks, and use them as an intermediate representation for predicting the complete output.

The method learns two mappings. The first predicts the selected landmark outputs from the input. The second predicts all output dimensions from those landmarks. Composing them produces the overall predictor. This arrangement makes selected parts of the output serve a dual purpose: they are prediction targets themselves and the basis for estimating the remaining output structure.

The authors state that the resulting conditional model has favorable statistical properties. Classification and regression experiments on multiple datasets show it outperforming one-versus-all prediction and several more sophisticated multiple-output methods. The findings support the idea that a carefully selected subset of outputs can provide an effective bridge between the input and a much larger collection of predictions.
icml-2012-the-landmark-selection-method-.tldr: Predicting a small set of landmark outputs first provides an effective intermediate step for high-dimensional multiple-output prediction.
